scene-u01-pnew1-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew1-26.text: KP11 changed which neurons are present; this unit changes what values enter each layer.

scene-u01-pnew1-28.name: text#28
scene-u01-pnew1-28.text: Each time earlier layers' weights update, the input distribution seen by a later layer changes.

scene-u01-pnew1-30.name: text#30
scene-u01-pnew1-30.text: Like an exam whose difficulty changes every day: hard to learn steadily.

scene-u01-pnew1-32.name: text#32
scene-u01-pnew1-32.text:
Method: for each mini-batch and each feature (or neuron input) standardize separately
to mean $0$ and variance $1$.

scene-u01-pnew1-61.name: text#61
scene-u01-pnew1-61.text: one ruler for every layer's input!

scene-u01-pnew1-63.name: text#63
scene-u01-pnew1-63.text: Batch normalization: first steady the input on one ruler.

scene-u01-pnew2-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew2-26.text: A mini-batch has $b$ data points; feature $j$ of point $i$ is $x_{ij}$.

scene-u01-pnew2-30.name: text#30
scene-u01-pnew2-30.text: mean of feature $j$ over this batch

scene-u01-pnew2-40.name: text#40
scene-u01-pnew2-40.text: Every feature $j$ gets its own $\mu_j$, $\sigma_j^2$, independent of the others.

scene-u01-pnew2-42.name: text#42
scene-u01-pnew2-42.text: If a feature is constant in the batch, $\sigma_j^2=0$: $\varepsilon$ keeps it from blowing up.

scene-u01-pnew3-57.name: text#57
scene-u01-pnew3-57.text: With $\varepsilon=0$ the values are $\pm1.341641,\ \pm0.447214$; $\varepsilon$ only touches the 6th decimal (max gap $1.3\times10^{-6}$).

scene-u01-pnew3-61.name: text#61
scene-u01-pnew3-61.text: The four values are moved to centre $0$, std about $1$.

scene-u01-pnew4-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew4-25.text: A bonus: the unit and size of a feature no longer matter

scene-u01-pnew4-38.name: text#38
scene-u01-pnew4-38.text: After standardizing the two features are identical (max gap $1.3\times10^{-6}$): $-1.3416,\ -0.4472,\ 0.4472,\ 1.3416$.

scene-u01-pnew4-40.name: text#40
scene-u01-pnew4-40.text: Two features differing $100$-fold arrive at the next layer equally large.

scene-u01-pnew5-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew5-25.text: But it only fixes mean and variance; the shape stays

scene-u01-pnew5-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew5-26.text: A skewed feature: $1000$ log-normal points (fixed seed).

scene-u01-pnew5-95.name: text#95
scene-u01-pnew5-95.text: The shape is identical; skewness is $2.7898$ before and after.

scene-u01-pnew5-97.name: text#97
scene-u01-pnew5-97.text: Small example $1,1,2,2,3,10$: skewness $1.6043$ before and after; the outlier $10$ moves to $2.1822$.

scene-u01-pnew5-99.name: text#99
scene-u01-pnew5-99.text: It shifts and rescales; it never turns skewed into symmetric.

scene-u01-pnew6-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew6-25.text: After standardizing, add a learnable scale and shift

scene-u01-pnew6-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew6-26.text: Added: the source omits this step but practical batch normalization always has it.

scene-u01-pnew6-30.name: text#30
scene-u01-pnew6-30.text: $\gamma_j$ (scale), $\beta_j$ (shift) are learned by gradient descent like weights.

scene-u01-pnew6-32.name: text#32
scene-u01-pnew6-32.text: Why? Forcing mean $0$, variance $1$ is not always what this layer needs.

scene-u01-pnew6-34.name: text#34
scene-u01-pnew6-34.text: If $\gamma_j=\sqrt{\sigma_j^2+\varepsilon}$ and $\beta_j=\mu_j$, this step restores the original input: no expressiveness is lost.

scene-u01-pnew6-38.name: text#38
scene-u01-pnew6-38.text: Standardize first, then let the network choose how big and how shifted.

scene-u01-pnew7-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew7-25.text: At test time? Use the moving average gathered in training

scene-u01-pnew7-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew7-26.text: Added: training and test behave differently, just like dropout.

scene-u01-pnew7-32.name: text#32
scene-u01-pnew7-32.text: We may predict one point at a time, so batch statistics are meaningless; the same point should not get different answers depending on its batch.

scene-u01-pnew7-36.name: text#36
scene-u01-pnew7-36.text: Update a little each batch ($m$ a small momentum constant); at test time use these fixed values. PyTorch switches with model.train() / model.eval().

scene-u01-pnew7-38.name: text#38
scene-u01-pnew7-38.text: At test time: fixed moving averages, ignoring batch neighbours.

scene-u01-pnew8-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew8-25.text: Why does it work? Mainly not by "steadying the input distribution"

scene-u01-pnew8-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew8-26.text: This page cites a single study and does not redo its analysis.

scene-u01-pnew8-28.name: text#28
scene-u01-pnew8-28.text: Early explanation: reducing covariate shift (layer input distributions drifting during training).

scene-u01-pnew8-33.name: text#33
scene-u01-pnew8-33.text: Later research: the main benefit is a smoother loss landscape: loss changes more gently with parameters, gradients are more predictable, so larger learning rates and steadier training.

scene-u01-pnew8-37.name: text#37
scene-u01-pnew8-37.text: So: do not take "steadying the input distribution" as the reason it works. The intuition of page 1 is only an intuition.

scene-u01-pnew8-39.name: text#39
scene-u01-pnew8-39.text: The main reason: a smoother loss landscape.

scene-u01-pnew9-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew9-25.text: Batch statistics are noisy: the smaller the batch, the noisier

scene-u01-pnew9-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew9-26.text: An $N(0,1)$ feature, $5000$ batches for each batch size (fixed seed).

scene-u01-pnew9-76.name: text#76
scene-u01-pnew9-76.text: std of the batch mean $=1/\sqrt b$

scene-u01-pnew9-82.name: text#82
scene-u01-pnew9-82.text: Small batches underestimate the std and add noise: a mild regularization, no substitute for dropout.

scene-u01-pnew10-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew10-25.text: When it breaks: batches too small, the extreme is $b=1$

scene-u01-pnew10-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew10-26.text: With a single data point $x$: the mean is the point itself.

scene-u01-pnew10-35.name: text#35
scene-u01-pnew10-35.text: Every data point is standardized to $0$; all information vanishes.

scene-u01-pnew10-37.name: text#37
scene-u01-pnew10-37.text: So a large enough batch is needed (usually tens of points); with tiny batches use batch-independent normalization (beyond this unit).

scene-u01-pnew10-39.name: text#39
scene-u01-pnew10-39.text: Smaller batches are not better: too small and the statistics are unreliable.

scene-u01-pnew11-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew11-25.text: Chapter review: what each method controls

scene-u01-pnew11-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew11-26.text: The shared problem: doing well on training data does not mean doing well on new data.

scene-u01-pnew11-62.name: text#62
scene-u01-pnew11-62.text: All methods do one thing: lower effective complexity or variance without adding much bias.

scene-u01-pnew12-25.text: The chapter's thread, and the next chapter

scene-u01-pnew12-26.text: Week 4 in one sentence: doing well on training data does not mean doing well on new data.

scene-u01-pnew12-30.text: Either lower effective complexity: $\ell_2$, $\ell_1$, early stopping.

steps.label: KP12 · 1/12
steps.speakerNotes: KP11's dropout changed which neurons are present; this unit changes what values enter each layer. Each time earlier layers' weights update, the input distribution of a later layer changes, like an exam whose difficulty changes daily: hard to learn steadily. (This is only an intuition; later we see it is not why batch normalization works.)

steps.label: KP12 · 1/12 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: KP11's dropout changed which neurons are present; this unit changes what values enter each layer. Each time earlier layers' weights update, the input distribution of a later layer changes, like an exam whose difficulty changes daily: hard to learn steadily. (This is only an intuition; later we see it is not why batch normalization works.)

steps.label: KP12 · 1/12 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The method is direct: for each mini-batch and each feature or neuron input, standardize separately to mean 0 and variance 1.

steps.label: KP12 · 1/12 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: That is, put every layer's input on the same ruler.

steps.label: KP12 · 2/12
steps.speakerNotes: First the mean of feature j over this batch: μ_j = (1/b) Σ x_ij.

steps.label: KP12 · 2/12 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: First the mean of feature j over this batch: μ_j = (1/b) Σ x_ij.

steps.label: KP12 · 2/12 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Then the variance σ_j² = (1/b) Σ (x_ij − μ_j)², divided by b not b − 1: the source's convention and KP02's population variance.

steps.label: KP12 · 2/12 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally standardize: x̂_ij = (x_ij − μ_j) / √(σ_j² + ε). ε has one job: if a feature is the same for every point in the batch, σ_j² = 0 and the denominator would be 0; a tiny ε (e.g. 10⁻⁵) prevents that and otherwise changes the result almost invisibly. Each feature is computed separately.

steps.label: KP12 · 3/12 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Before standardizing the four points lie between 2 and 8.

steps.label: KP12 · 3/12 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: After: (−1.3416, −0.4472, 0.4472, 1.3416). With ε = 0 the values are ±1.341641, ±0.447214; the max gap is only 1.3 × 10⁻⁶, ε touches just the sixth decimal. The new mean is 0; the new variance σ²/(σ² + ε) = 0.999998, slightly below 1, also due to ε. (Computed in code.)

steps.label: KP12 · 4/12
steps.speakerNotes: Feature 1 is 2, 4, 6, 8: mean 5, variance 5.

steps.label: KP12 · 4/12 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Feature 1 is 2, 4, 6, 8: mean 5, variance 5.

steps.label: KP12 · 4/12 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Feature 2 is 100 times that: 200, 400, 600, 800; mean 500, variance 50000.

steps.label: KP12 · 4/12 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: After standardizing the values are exactly the same as above, max gap 1.3 × 10⁻⁶. Two features differing a hundredfold arrive at the next layer equally large. (Added, computed in code.)

steps.label: KP12 · 5/12
steps.speakerNotes: Left: the skewed feature before standardizing: 1000 log-normal points, mean 2.15, std 1.91, long right tail. (Re-run with the lecture figure script's seed; horizontal range cut to 0–14 as in the lecture.)

steps.label: KP12 · 5/12 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Left: the skewed feature before standardizing: 1000 log-normal points, mean 2.15, std 1.91, long right tail. (Re-run with the lecture figure script's seed; horizontal range cut to 0–14 as in the lecture.)

steps.label: KP12 · 5/12 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Right: after standardizing, mean 0, std 1.

steps.label: KP12 · 5/12 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The two histograms have exactly the same shape: same peak, same tail, skewness 2.7898 in both. Small example 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 10 (b = 6): mean 3.1667, variance 9.8056, standardized (−0.6919, −0.6919, −0.3726, −0.3726, −0.0532, 2.1822); skewness 1.6043 before and after; the right-tail outlier is still there. Batch normalization shifts and rescales; it does not turn a skewed distribution symmetric.

steps.label: KP12 · 6/12
steps.speakerNotes: Standardizing forces each layer's input to mean 0, variance 1, which is not always what the layer needs; e.g. before a sigmoid, inputs near 0 make the function nearly linear. So a learnable linear map y = γ x̂ + β follows. (Added: the source omits this step.) γ (scale) and β (shift) are learned by gradient descent like other weights.

steps.label: KP12 · 6/12 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Standardizing forces each layer's input to mean 0, variance 1, which is not always what the layer needs; e.g. before a sigmoid, inputs near 0 make the function nearly linear. So a learnable linear map y = γ x̂ + β follows. (Added: the source omits this step.) γ (scale) and β (shift) are learned by gradient descent like other weights.

steps.label: KP12 · 6/12 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: If γ = √(σ² + ε) and β = μ, this step exactly restores the original input, so it loses no expressiveness; it just makes the layer input's mean and scale two directly learnable parameters.

steps.label: KP12 · 6/12 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Example: 2, 4, 6, 8 with γ = 2, β = 1 give y = (−1.6833, 0.1056, 1.8944, 3.6833), mean 1, std 2. (Computed in code.)

steps.label: KP12 · 7/12
steps.speakerNotes: In training μ_j, σ_j² come from the current batch.

steps.label: KP12 · 7/12 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: In training μ_j, σ_j² come from the current batch.

steps.label: KP12 · 7/12 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: At test time we may predict one point at a time; one point gives no meaningful batch statistics, and the same data point should not get different answers depending on who shares its batch.

steps.label: KP12 · 7/12 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The usual way: during training also keep moving averages of μ and σ², updating a little each batch with μ̄ ← (1−m) μ̄ + m μ_batch (m a small momentum constant), and use these fixed values at test time. Like dropout, training and test behave differently, switched in PyTorch by model.train() and model.eval(). (Added; not in the source.)

steps.label: KP12 · 8/12
steps.speakerNotes: The early explanation was reducing covariate shift, i.e. the drift of layer input distributions during training; the source of the intuition on page 1.

steps.label: KP12 · 8/12 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The early explanation was reducing covariate shift, i.e. the drift of layer input distributions during training; the source of the intuition on page 1.

steps.label: KP12 · 8/12 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The source says later research shows this explanation is not right; the main benefit is a smoother loss landscape: the loss changes more gently with the parameters, gradients are more predictable, so larger learning rates and steadier training are possible. The conclusion is from Santurkar et al., NeurIPS 2018 (added).

steps.label: KP12 · 8/12 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: We do not redo that analysis here; just remember: do not take steadying the input distribution as the reason it works.

steps.label: KP12 · 9/12 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: For an N(0,1) feature, draw 5000 batches for each batch size and compute the batch std (blue line, band ±1 std) and the spread of the batch mean (orange line). (Re-run with the lecture figure script's seed; numbers match exactly.)

steps.label: KP12 · 9/12 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The std of the batch mean is 1/√b: b = 4 gives 0.4912, b = 16 gives 0.2482, b = 64 gives 0.1270, b = 256 gives 0.0622.

steps.label: KP12 · 9/12 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The mean batch std also differs from the true 1: b = 4 gives 0.7878, b = 16 gives 0.9539, b = 256 gives 0.9964, underestimating for small batches. The smaller the batch the noisier, which adds a little noise to each layer's input: a mild regularization, but not strong enough to replace dropout. Empirically, with batch normalization dropout can often be reduced or dropped (common practice, not a theorem).

steps.label: KP12 · 10/12
steps.speakerNotes: Too-small batches give unreliable statistics (previous page). Extreme b = 1: one data point, the mean is itself, σ² = 0.

steps.speakerNotes: Every data point is standardized to 0 and all information vanishes. (Checked in code.) So batch normalization needs large enough batches, usually tens of points; for tiny batches or when batching is inconvenient, use other batch-independent normalization, beyond this unit.

steps.label: KP12 · 11/12 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Data splits and cross-validation (KP01, KP06) evaluate honestly without changing the model; ℓ2 and weight decay (KP07, KP08) shrink weights and ℓ1 (KP09) creates sparsity, both lower effective complexity and act on the objective; early stopping (KP10) trains less, roughly ℓ2, acting on the training process.

steps.label: KP12 · 11/12 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Dropout (KP11) lowers variance, approximating the sub-network average, acting on hidden layers; batch normalization (KP12) steadies and smooths optimization with a mild regularization, acting between layers. The chapter's one-line thread: true error ≈ training error + complexity, so either lower the effective complexity or lower the variance.

steps.label: KP12 · 12/12
steps.speakerNotes: The chapter's thread in one sentence: true error ≈ training error + complexity.

steps.label: KP12 · 12/12 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The chapter's thread in one sentence: true error ≈ training error + complexity.

steps.label: KP12 · 12/12 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: So either lower the effective complexity (ℓ2, ℓ1, early stopping) or lower the variance (dropout), with batch normalization steadying optimization; every regularization method achieves this in a different way without adding much bias. This is the meaning of the source's chapter summary, put into the language built in this chapter. (Added synthesis.)

steps.label: KP12 · 12/12 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Most methods of this chapter do not assume a particular network structure. The next chapter looks at a network that exploits the structure of data (locality and translation invariance of images): the convolutional neural network. Its kernels share weights and look only locally, another way to lower complexity; every idea of this chapter will reappear on the new structure.
